entities.summary: Astrometry, the ancient branch of astronomy, emerged during the Classical Era (5th century BCE to 5th century CE) as a crucial tool for understanding celestial bodies and their movements. This discipline allowed ancient Greek astronomers, such as Hipparchus and Ptolemy, to create detailed star catalogs, measure planetary orbits, and predict celestial events. By examining the relationships between the Earth, Sun, and stars, astrometry laid the groundwork for later scientific discoveries, including the development of trigonometry and the foundations of modern astronomy. The significance of astrometry can be seen in its influence on the work of later astronomers, such as Copernicus and Galileo, and its continued relevance in modern astrophysics and space exploration. The legacy of astrometry can be seen in the continued use of star catalogs and planetary orbits in modern astronomy, as well as its impact on the development of navigation and timekeeping. The ancient Greeks' fascination with the stars and their movements also reflects the enduring human desire to understand the universe and our place within it.
